Luke includes his own despair with the pronouns.
41.question: Luke admits the whole company, narrator included, gave up hope. What does honest despair inside a faithful story do for your own storms?

41.title: It Is Because of This Night
41.context: Paul's standing up is the storm's hinge, and his speech carries the angelic word with an administrator's precision: ship lost, cargo lost, no life lost, because 'you must stand before Caesar.' The famous 'I believe God, that it will turn out exactly as I have been told' is spoken by a prisoner to the professionals who ignored him, and the crew takes heart from the prisoner, Luke says, in the book's sharpest role reversal.
41.question: Paul believed God for the outcome while expecting the ship to be lost. What are you trusting God to keep, having surrendered what he has not promised to keep?

41.title: He Took Bread and Gave Thanks
41.context: Fourteen days of fasting fear, four anchors from the stern against the rocks, a sailors' escape attempt Paul checkmates with a sentence ('Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved'), and then the book's most ordinary miracle scene: a prisoner distributing bread to 276 people, giving thanks to God in the presence of all, before the lightened ship sails for the beach.
41.question: Paul's faith at the climax takes the form of breakfast for everyone. What ordinary provision is faith asking you to share calmly today?

41.title: All Were Brought Safely to Land
41.context: The centurion's counter-order saves every prisoner from the soldiers' plan to kill them, repaying, in the crisis, every kindness the voyage had built: Julius protects the man whose God protected the ship. Luke's arithmetic closes: some on planks, some on debris, all 276 ashore, not one life lost of the company the angel granted Paul. The ship is the only casualty.
41.question: The prisoners lived because one officer vetoed the convenient cruelty. Whose veto, spoken or unspoken, has protected you?

42.title: Barbarians Showing Extraordinary Kindness
42.context: Luke calls Malta's islanders 'barbarians,' the Greek word for non-Greek speakers, then praises their extraordinary kindness in the same breath. The viper scene plays their theology like a balance scale, murderer fated by Justice, then no harm, then a god, and Luke neither confirms nor corrects them; Paul's work there is firewood gathered like any man's.
42.question: Malta judged Paul twice in an afternoon and missed both times. How quickly do you swing your judgment of a person with their fortunes?

42.title: The Father of Publius
42.context: Publius, the island's leading man, hosts the shipwrecked company three days before Paul is brought to his father's sickroom; the order is Luke's: kindness received first, healing given second. The islanders' honors and the supplies loaded at departure mean the grain ship's loss ends in surplus, a company that arrived with nothing sailing away provisioned by the healed.
42.question: The islanders honored Paul with supplies because their chief's father recovered. What has gratitude provisioned in your own journeys?

42.title: He Thanked God and Took Courage
42.context: The Dioscuri, twin-god figureheads for sailors' luck, carry the ship of the man who announced no life would be lost in a greater storm than legend assigned them. Brothers from Rome walk forty miles down the Appian Way to meet a prisoner most have never seen, and the apostle who wrote 'I have many people in this city' now takes courage at the sight of some of them, still human enough to need it.
42.question: Paul took courage from simply seeing the brothers. Whose mere presence has restored your nerve for a task, and do they know it?

42.title: For the Hope of Israel I Wear This Chain
42.context: Three days after arrival, before any accuser lands, Paul briefs Rome's Jewish leaders himself: no crime against people or customs, Roman examiners willing to release, and the chain's true caption, the hope of Israel. Their reply is the book's most civil exchange: no letters, no reports, only curiosity about a sect spoken against everywhere, and a request to hear him.
42.question: Paul's self-summary in Rome is 'the hope of Israel' as the reason for a chain. How would you caption your own hardest constraint in the language of hope?

42.title: Preaching the Kingdom, Unhindered
42.context: The all-day session runs morning to evening and ends, as so many scenes have, divided: some persuaded, some disbelieving. Paul's final quoted Scripture is Isaiah 6, the hardening passage, and his final sentence sends salvation to the Gentiles 'and they will listen,' the book closing its first-circle and last-circle promises in one breath. Two whole years follow in a rented house, all comers received, the kingdom preached boldly and, in Luke's last word for the mission, unhindered, the open ending handed to every reader since.
42.question: Luke ends Acts without ending Paul's story. What unfinished story of yours might be an open ending rather than a missing one?
